title: runtime-contributor-onboarding-lab-guide-2026
author: Aisha Romero
content:
Summary
-------
This lab-style guide is intended to onboard new contributors and rotating engineers into the serving runtime team. It consolidates the minimum safe workflow for making experimental changes, running targeted profiling and benchmarks, exercising scheduler/kernels in sandboxes, and shipping small iterate-able improvements with maintained SLOs. The guide is written for engineers with prior Linux and Python experience; no prior kernel-development experience is required.

Audience
--------
- New members of eng-serving-runtime (runtime, kernel, scheduler, and tooling subteams)
- Rotating SREs and performance engineers who will run experiments or triage incidents

Why this exists
----------------
- Reduce time-to-meaningful-contribution while minimizing risk to production pools
- Establish reproducible experiments and artifact capture for each change
- Ensure every contributor follows the same safety, observability, and rollback gates

Prerequisites (local and cloud)
------------------------------
1. GitHub account with repo access: request via infra-oncall ticket if missing.
2. Bastion + kubectl access to dev clusters: dev-serving-1 and dev-serving-2.
3. GPU-enabled dev nodes (tag: runtime-lab) provisioned by infra.
4. Python 3.10 environment with dev dependencies: pip install -r tools/requirements.txt
5. Familiarity with the following playbooks: the runtime profiling playbook, kernel scheduling contract, and the canary-run matrix (links in "Related pages" above).

Quick environment setup (copy-paste)
-----------------------------------
# Create virtualenv and install
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -U pip setuptools
pip install -r tools/requirements.txt

# Configure kube context and dev cluster port-forwarding
export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config
kubectl config use-context dev-serving-1
# port-forward dispatcher for local profiling UI
kubectl -n runtime port-forward svc/dispatcher 8080:8080 &

Local sandbox: starting a single-shard runtime for experiments\-----------------------------------------------------------
We maintain a lightweight developer runtime image that mirrors production behavior but restricts capacity. Use this to iterate fast:

# start a single-node sandbox (local dev box must be in dev cluster)
kubectl -n runtime apply -f infra/k8s/sandbox-single-shard.yaml
kubectl -n runtime rollout status deploy/sandbox-runtime --timeout=120s

Once the sandbox is up, you can push model binaries to the sandbox bucket and point the runtime at them for kernel experiments.

Experiment lifecycle (minimum viable experiment)
------------------------------------------------
1) Hypothesis & test plan (commit to a small MD file under experiments/): include the expected metric delta and the signal source (trace, histogram, microbenchmark).
2) Local reproduction: run an isolated microbenchmark against sandbox using workload-replay tool.
3) Capture artifacts: profiling traces, kernel counters, target traces, and the synthetic corpus used. Attach artifacts to the experiment PR.
4) Peer review: request at least one reviewer from the kernel or runtime team depending on the change.
5) Canary run: run change in canary pool with trace sampling enabled and compare SLOs.
6) Rollout gate evaluation: use the rollout checklist (section below).
7) Roll forward or rollback based on gate results.

Profiling quick-start (what to collect and why)
------------------------------------------------
- Flame traces (CPU path) — to attribute host scheduling cost.
- GPU kernel timeline (nsight/metric export) — to find stalls or serialization.
- Kernel dispatch histograms (per-kernel latency P50/P90/P99).
- KV cache hit/miss counters and session lifecycle traces.
- Request and token level latency breakdown (dispatcher, kernel queue, kernel run).

Collecting a trace (example commands)
------------------------------------
# run the replay harness for 5 minutes and collect traces
replay --config experiments/basic-replay.yaml --duration 300 --trace-out artifacts/trace-$(date +%s).zip

# extract kernel counters from the node (requires node SSH)
ssh gpu-dev-node-1 sudo /opt/runtime/bin/pull-counters --out artifacts/counters-$(date +%s).json

Benchmarks: recommended suite and how to run
-------------------------------------------
We maintain a curated benchmark suite that mirrors common customer workloads. Benchmarks are separated into three categories: micro (kernel-level), meso (single-model end-to-end on a shard), and e2e (multi-tenant dispatcher+shard).

Running a microbenchmark (example)
1. Build kernel hint artifact: make -C runtime/kernel artifacts/bench_hint.o
2. Run microbench: python tools/microbench.py --kernel bench_hint.o --iters 1000 --out artifacts/micro-$(date +%s).json

Running the meso benchmark (dispatcher + single shard)
1. kubectl -n runtime apply -f infra/k8s/bench-meso.yaml
2. python tools/bench_driver.py --scenario meso-latency --duration 600 --sample-rate 100

SLOs and safety gates for experiments
------------------------------------
- Baseline SLOs (applies to all experiments unless otherwise noted):
  - P99 end-to-end latency (single-token): <= 250ms on dev shards
  - P95 inference latency (per request): <= 180ms
  - Error rate (HTTP 5xx): <= 0.05% in canary
  - Kernel regressions: no increase > 5% P99 kernel-run-time vs baseline for the same sequence-length distribution

Gate checklist (before canary)
1. Unit tests and microbench suite pass locally.
2. Profiling artifacts attached to PR.
3. Performance regression test (meso benchmark) within threshold.
4. Observability: trace sampling enabled and dashboards updated.
5. Rollout plan with timeboxed canary and rollback TTL.

Canary run matrix (example)
--------------------------
- Canary group A: 1 shard, 10% production trace sampling, 12-hour run, synthetic and shadow traffic.
- Canary group B: 2 shards, real production traffic at 1%, 24-hour run, enhanced telemetry.

Rollback triggers (automated/manual)
------------------------------------
- Automated: error rate exceeds 0.1% OR P99 latency regresses by > 10% sustained for 5 minutes.
- Manual: on-call or owning engineer observes customer-visible degradation or fidelity regression.

Making kernel changes: additional cautions
------------------------------------------
- Kernel patches must include deterministic microbench and counter-driven rationale.
- Avoid changes that alter kernel ABI or input serialization without explicit compat notes.
- Include a fallback path (config flag) to switch back to previous kernel implementation at runtime.

Example CI job for kernel change (YAML snippet)
------------------------------------------------
ci-jobs:
  kernel-change-check:
    steps:
      - name: run-unit-tests
        run: make test
      - name: run-microbench
        run: python tools/microbench.py --iters 200 --out artifacts/ci-micro.json
      - name: upload-artifacts
        run: ./tools/ci/upload-artifacts artifacts/ci-micro.json
      - name: auto-profile-compare
        run: python tools/ci/compare_profiles.py --baseline s3://bench-baselines/kernel-p99.json --candidate artifacts/ci-micro.json
\nPost-merge observability and ownership
--------------------------------------
- Ownership: the author owns the change for a 72-hour burn-in period. The oncall takes secondary watches.
- Dashboards: add a dashboard panel named feature/<pr-number> to the Runtime Canary folder.
- Alerts: for short-lived experiments use an alert muting policy; create a tagging rule to ensure faster triage.

Runbook snippets and playbook links
----------------------------------
- If kernel stall is suspected: follow the "kernel-stability-siege-testing" playbook (see Related pages) and collect GPU timelines, host traces, and allocator stats.
- For cross-tenant noise: consult the "multi-tenant-affinity-noise-mitigation" benchmark procedures.

Checklist for turning an experiment into a permanent change
----------------------------------------------------------
1. Confirm that artifacts, benchmarks, and canary runs are reproducible and archived.
2. Update runtime feature flags or configuration schema.
3. Add automated microbench to CI with the new baseline.
4. Document the change in release notes and link to experiment artifacts.
5. Schedule a follow-up verification run after 30 days.

Roles & responsibilities (table)
--------------------------------
| Role | Responsibility | Escalation |
|---|---|---|
| Author | Write experiment plan, implement change, run local CI | Team lead |
| Reviewer | Validate benchmarks and safety gates | Senior runtime engineer |
| Oncall | Monitor canary, trigger rollback if thresholds hit | SRE lead |
| Bench steward | Maintain benchmark baselines and runner infra | Performance lead |

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
------------------------------------
- Pitfall: running benchmarks with mismatched sequence-length distributions.
  Remedy: verify input corpus stats with tools/corpus_stats.py and attach results.
- Pitfall: forgetting to enable trace sampling in canary.
  Remedy: use the canary template from infra/canary-templates/canary-config.yaml.
- Pitfall: not including a fallback flag for kernel ABIs.
  Remedy: always add a runtime toggle and document expected behavior.

Appendix A: Useful commands and tooling paths
--------------------------------------------
- replay: tools/replay/README.md
- microbench: tools/microbench.py
- profiler UI: http://localhost:8080 (port-forward to dispatcher)
- trace archive convention: experiments/<pr-number>/artifacts/<timestamp>.zip

Appendix B: On-call contacts and escalation matrix
--------------------------------------------------
- Runtime oncall (primary): #eng-runtime-oncall Slack
- Performance lead: lena@redwood.ai
- Kernel lead: theo@redwood.ai

Related pages
-------------
See the profiling playbook, kernel scheduling contracts, and the benchmarking suite for deeper reference material. This page is the operational glue that explains how to safely move through the change lifecycle from idea to production.
